Worker larvae of the Argentine ant (Linepithema humile) hatch after an incubation period of roughly 16.0 days [ab = roughly 16.0 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a developmental rate that aligns with the rapid colony expansion characteristic of this invasive species. At the moment of hatching, the newly emerged first-instar larva measures just 0.03 cm [Lb = 0.03 cm] in body length, making it one of the smallest neonate stages among the Dolichoderinae. This initial wet weight at birth has been recorded as 0.00002 grams [Ww0 = 0.00002 grams], a value reflecting the minimal yolk reserves provisioned in the egg. The larva then enters a period of accelerated somatic growth, feeding voraciously on trophallactically distributed food within the nest. This phase of rapid mass increase continues until the larva reaches a length of approximately 0.44 cm , measured through the spiracles at the end of the acceleration phase. The time from hatching to this developmental milestone is 45.0 days  under the same thermal regime of 28 °C at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Following the completion of larval growth, the insect undergoes a holometabolic transformation within a silken cocoon. The non-feeding pupal stage, during which imaginal disc differentiation and histolysis of larval tissues occur, culminates in pupal completion and subsequent emergence as a teneral adult. The interval from the onset of pupation to the moment of adult eclosion, measured on worker pupae, has been determined to be 9.0 days  at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a brief interval that reflects the accelerated holometabolic development typical of worker castes, minimizing the non-feeding vulnerable pupal period. The freshly emerged imago, or callow worker, is initially pale and soft-bodied, but it quickly undergoes cuticle hardening and sclerotisation. At this point of imago emergence, the body length of the adult worker ranges from 0.45 to 0.5 cm, with a reported imaginal length of 0.475 cm . This size places Linepithema humile among the smaller formicine ants, a trait that facilitates its ability to infiltrate and dominate new territories.

The mass of the adult ant increases considerably from the neonatal stage due to the accumulation of structural tissues and fat reserves. The wet weight of the imago, measured immediately after eclosion from emerged gynes (reproductive females), has been recorded at 0.00277 grams . The corresponding dry weight of the imago, obtained after desiccation of the same specimens, is 0.00068 grams , indicating a substantial water content typical of soft-bodied teneral insects. These mass measurements are critical for understanding the energetic investment that colonies make in producing reproductive individuals. In comparison to worker ants, which are generally lighter and more streamlined, the gynes represent a significant allocation of colony resources, a factor that likely influences the timing and frequency of reproductive events within the colony's annual cycle.

The longevity of reproductive individuals in this species presents an interesting paradox due to intense social dynamics. While worker ants face high mortality from predation and inter-colony aggression, queens can persist for several years. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 28 °C, the maximum recorded lifespan for a Linepithema humile queen is approximately four years, equating to 1461.0 days [am = 1461.0 days] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This extended lifespan is remarkable given that the vast majority of workers are executed by their nestmates within their first year, a behavior known as worker policing or execution. The queen's longevity allows her to produce a continuous stream of offspring, building colossal supercolonies that can span hundreds of kilometers. This reproductive strategy, coupled with a relatively short generation time, underpins the species' extraordinary invasive success across Mediterranean and subtropical ecosystems.

Comparative analysis of body size and mass at key developmental transitions reveals the efficiency of the Argentine ant's life history within the context of supercolony energetics. The imaginal length of approximately 0.475 cm  represents more than a fifteen-fold increase from the 0.03 cm [Lb = 0.03 cm] length at birth, illustrating the dramatic allometric shifts occurring during larval development. Similarly, the wet mass increases from the initial 0.00002 grams [Ww0 = 0.00002 grams] of the newly hatched larva to the emerged imago's wet weight of 0.00277 grams , a gain of over two orders of magnitude. The dry weight of the imago, 0.00068 grams , represents the structural investment retained after water loss, a metric useful for comparing metabolic efficiency across ant species. The capacity to achieve a length at the end of the acceleration phase of 0.44 cm  within a brief period of 45.0 days  at 28 °C underscores the highly optimized growth physiology that enables this ant to rapidly exploit ephemeral resources and outcompete native species at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].
